topic: Improving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for question answering

selected_papers.title: ChunkRank: Relevance-Weighted Passage Selection for RAG
selected_papers.abstract: We propose ChunkRank, a lightweight reranking step that scores retrieved passages by relevance to the query before they are shown to a generation model. On two short-context QA benchmarks, ChunkRank improves answer accuracy over a standard top-k retrieval baseline, with a small added latency cost from the reranking step. All experiments use single-hop, English-language questions.

selected_papers.title: LongMem: Compressive Memory for Multi-Hop Retrieval
selected_papers.abstract: LongMem introduces a compressive memory module that lets a retrieval system summarize and reuse information across multiple retrieval hops instead of re-retrieving from scratch each time. On a multi-hop QA benchmark, LongMem improves accuracy over single-hop retrieval baselines, but adds noticeably higher inference latency due to the memory compression step. Evaluation is limited to English-language corpora.

selected_papers.title: CiteGuard: Faithfulness Verification for Generated Answers
selected_papers.abstract: CiteGuard is a post-hoc verifier that checks whether each sentence of a generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved passages it cites, flagging unsupported sentences before the answer is shown to a user. Applying CiteGuard reduces the rate of unsupported claims in generated answers, at the cost of an extra inference pass per answer. The verifier itself is not evaluated on multi-hop or non-English questions.

approved_web_articles.title: Why Chunk Ranking Matters for RAG Pipelines in Production
approved_web_articles.snippet: Teams running retrieval-augmented generation in production report that a simple relevance-ranking pass over retrieved chunks, before generation, meaningfully reduces off-topic citations -- without needing a larger retrieval model.

executive_summary.content: Three recent techniques address distinct failure points in retrieval-augmented generation: passage-level reranking (ChunkRank), cross-hop memory compression (LongMem), and post-hoc answer verification (CiteGuard). ChunkRank and LongMem each report a measured accuracy gain against their own added computational cost; CiteGuard reports a reduction in unsupported claims against its own added cost. None benchmarks its trade-off jointly with the others, and none evaluates outside English, single-domain QA.

introduction_scope.content: This review covers exactly three papers selected for this topic, spanning three distinct intervention points in a RAG pipeline: what gets retrieved (ChunkRank), how retrieval state persists across hops (LongMem), and whether the final answer is verifiably supported (CiteGuard). No broader survey of RAG methods is attempted.

thematic_findings.content: ChunkRank and LongMem both target the retrieval side of the pipeline but at different granularities: ChunkRank re-scores an already-retrieved passage set for relevance before generation, improving accuracy on single-hop questions [1], while LongMem changes what persists across multiple retrieval steps via compressive memory, improving accuracy on multi-hop questions [2]. Read together, they suggest the accuracy gain from 'using retrieved content better' generalizes across at least two different retrieval granularities, even though the two papers never test each other's setting. CiteGuard operates downstream of both, checking the generated answer's sentences against retrieved passages after generation rather than improving retrieval itself, and independently reduces the rate of unsupported claims [3].

methodology_landscape.content: ChunkRank's reranking step is applied independently of the base retriever, making it a composable add-on [1]. LongMem's compressive memory instead modifies the retrieval loop's internal state across steps, which is a more invasive integration than a bolt-on reranker [1][2]. CiteGuard makes no retrieval-time changes at all -- it is a strictly post-hoc check, which means it can in principle be layered on top of either ChunkRank or LongMem without conflicting with either's own mechanism [3], though none of the three papers actually tests that combination.

citation_correctness.label: pass
citation_correctness.rationale: Each [N] marker is attached to a claim its reference actually makes -- e.g. [2] LongMem is cited only for multi-hop accuracy/added latency, never for anything about verification or reranking.

groundedness.label: pass
groundedness.rationale: All claims (accuracy direction, relative cost framing, English-only scope, architectural composability as a claim about design, not a tested result) trace directly to abstract text or are explicitly framed as the report's own untested inference, not asserted as a finding.

synthesis_quality.label: pass
synthesis_quality.rationale: Methodology Landscape and Thematic Findings both compare the three papers against each other by theme/mechanism (granularity of intervention, composability) rather than listing each paper's contribution in isolation.

analytical_quality.label: pass
analytical_quality.rationale: Gap Analysis (no cross-technique composability measurement) is turned into a specific, non-duplicate proposal in Future Research Directions (a joint accuracy-vs-latency benchmark; testing CiteGuard against LongMem's own output) -- the two sections make distinct claims.

template_fit.label: pass
template_fit.rationale: Analytical-appropriate: no term is over-explained (no definition of 'retrieval' or 'faithfulness' the way the foundational version has), but the report still balances explanation with cross-paper synthesis rather than assuming expert-level familiarity.

coherence.label: pass
coherence.rationale: No sentence is repeated verbatim across sections; each section's claims build on, rather than restate, the previous section's (Contradictions references the trade-offs Methodology Landscape set up; Future Research Directions references the composability gap Gap Analysis named).

source_balance.label: pass
source_balance.rationale: All three papers appear in comparative roles across multiple sections; the single web source supports one specific claim in Future Research Directions rather than substituting for a paper citation anywhere.
